newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Pustovoitenko becomes Ukraine PM, reforms to stay.
newsitem.headline: Pustovoitenko becomes Ukraine PM, reforms to stay.

text.p: The Ukrainian parliament confirmed political pragmatist Valery Pustovoitenko as prime minister on Wednesday.
Addressing the chamber before the vote, the close ally of President Leonid Kuchma said Ukraine would stay on the track of economic reform.
He won the support of 226 deputies -- just attaining the absolute majority he needed in the 450-seat chamber. Ninety-one deputies voted against him.

Previously a minister without portfolio, the 50-year-old Pustovoitenko replaces Pavlo Lazarenko, who resigned earlier this month complaining about the state of his health -- although many analysts saw more political motives behind the move.

Kuchma said on Wednesday he had been unhappy with Lazarenko's performance in dealing with the economy and the damage to Ukraine's image caused by international media reports about corruption, in which Lazarenko was allegedly involved.

Kuchma, praising the result of the vote, told reporters that parliament would be more involved in the formation of the new government but declined to say what changes he intended to make in the cabinet.

Before the vote, Pustovoitenko said his main priorities would be stimulating private enterprises, reducing taxes and diminishing the size of the shadow economy, estimated in Ukraine at between 40 and 60 per cent of the whole economy.

Pustovoitenko also said he aimed to solve the problem of a huge backlog of unpaid wages, estimated at four billion hryvnias ($2.1 billion). Millions of state sector workers have not been paid for several months.
Combined with delays in pensions and student grants, the backlog stands at about 6.7 billion hryvnias ($3.6 billion).
"He is the only choice in current economic situation," Volodymyr Horbulin, a Secretary of the policy-making Security and Defence Counsil, told reporters.
"There is no reason for the West to worry that reforms won't be carried out actively. The direction is clear and is not going to be changed. But there might be some corrections," Horbulin added.
Pustovoitenko faces the tough task of getting an Extended Fund Facility, estimated at between $2.5-$3 billion, from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

A senior IMF official said on Wednesday that Ukraine was likely to get a smaller stand-by loan by the end of next month after two rounds of talks but added that it could be repleced with the bigger credit at a later date.
Some liberals and leftist opponents were sceptical about Pustovoitenko's ability to carry out market reforms.

"Pustovoitenko will build a normal, planned economy, favouring subsidies to state-owned enterprises," reformist deputy Serhiy Teryokhin told Reuters. "He has qualities acceptable for any regime with a planned economy."
"President Kuchma has already had three prime ministers (during his three-year term). Now he has got a fourth one," leading leftist Natalya Vitrenko told the chamber.
"Pustovoitenko is neither better not worse than his predecessors and there are no guarantees that president will not be unhappy with this choice in a month," she added.

Pustovoitenko, who is the seventh prime minister in the six years of Ukraine's post-Soviet history, is very close to Kuchma and is widely seen as pragmatic and as having good managerial experience and skills.
Between 1991-1993 Pustovoitenko used to be a mayor of Dnipropetrovsk, a powerful industrial base in eastern Ukraine and the home city of Kuchma and former Prime Minister Lazarenko.
